claims.text: The starting material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr starting material is in the as-cast state.
As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has approximately 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
Poor oxidation resistance limits use of HfNbTaTiZr at high temperature in air.
An anti-oxidation coating is a relevant intervention for enabling high-temperature application of this alloy system in air.
A silicide- or aluminide-based coating is specifically suitable for HfNbTaTiZr.
The protective coating should be 5–10 μm thick.
Pack cementation or chemical vapor deposition can produce the proposed coating on HfNbTaTiZr.
The engineered coating will form a stable SiO2 or Al2O3 scale.
The dense protective scale will impede inward oxygen transport at approximately 1000 °C in air.
Limiting oxygen infiltration will mitigate phase destabilization and embrittlement in the HfNbTaTiZr substrate.
The coating will remain oxidation-protective at 1000 °C in air for at least 100 hours.
After the proposed exposure, coated specimens will retain a yield strength in the range 163–530 MPa.
After the proposed exposure, coated specimens will retain at least 8% room-temperature tensile ductility.
The coated substrate will exhibit minimal oxide-scale formation.
Uncoated HfNbTaTiZr undergoes increasing oxidation and embrittlement during prolonged exposure to air at 1000 °C, reducing strength and ductility.
Coatings thinner than 5 μm may undergo localized spallation or cracking.
An excessively thick or poorly bonded coating can generate thermal-mismatch spalling or stress concentrations that reduce ductility.
Thermal-expansion mismatch, coating-substrate incompatibility, and brittle oxide scales may reduce strain tolerance in service.

contradictions.description: The conditions describe up to 100 hours of exposure under tensile loading at a specified strain rate, whereas the measurements describe tensile testing post-exposure. It is therefore unclear whether mechanical loading is simultaneous with oxidation or applied only after oxidation.
